timeline.event: UNESCO inscribed Aklan pina handloom weaving on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 6 December 2023.
Long pineapple leaf fibers up to about 70 cm were extracted from Azores pineapple waste, with 14 days of retting at 25 C giving the strongest fibers.
Enzyme-enhanced processing of pineapple leaf fiber was reported for green textile applications with natural dyeing.

timeline.event: Paper yarn was compared with cotton, viscose and polyester yarns on mechanical properties.
Surface treatments were shown to improve the knittability of paper yarn made from Swedish forest resources.
Two wood-pulp paper yarns kept about 89 to 95% of their breaking strength after 15 wash cycles.
A salt-free dyeing route for paper yarn used a cationic cellulose nanofiber and chitosan auxiliary.
Researchers adapted shifu techniques to make experimental fungal paper yarns.

timeline.event: Pacific paper mulberry, the main barkcloth plant, was carried from Taiwan by Austronesian-speaking voyagers, according to phylogeographic evidence.
Western explorers collected many decorated Pacific barkcloths, now used for dye and DNA studies.
UNESCO proclaimed barkcloth making in Uganda a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
A study characterized colorants used on Pacific barkcloths.
Dyes from Tahitian plants, including mati red, were identified in historical barkcloth.

timeline.event: Helical lotus-root fibers were used as templates for soft helical microswimmers.
Coiled lotus fiber yarn was made into an artificial muscle with a reversible tensile stroke of about 38% in response to water or humidity.
Researchers published an open design for an automatic lotus fiber extractor intended to raise productivity for hand workers.
